key_insight: The paper argues that AI development must adopt a 'strong sustainability' framework—treating natural capital as non‑substitutable and enforcing absolute ecological limits—so AI design, deployment and governance operate within planetary boundaries rather than assuming technological substitution will solve environmental harms.
problem_solved: Addresses the unchecked resource and material footprint of AI (energy, materials, lifecycle impacts) and the absence of limit‑based policy and design principles that ensure AI growth does not exceed ecological and social carrying capacities.
method: Translate strong sustainability principles into an AI‑specific framework: define non‑substitutable natural capitals and absolute ecological limits applicable to compute, energy and material use.

Develop metrics and lifecycle perspectives (manufacture → training → deployment → end‑of‑life), and propose allocation rules and guardrails (budgets, caps, priority uses) informed by planetary boundaries.
Recommend policy, governance and design levers (efficiency, reuse/circularity, sufficiency-oriented choices, procurement rules, reporting standards) to operationalize limits in practice.
impact: Shifts practitioner priorities from unconstrained performance scaling to designing within ecological budgets—enabling concrete decisions (model size, training frequency, hardware choices, reuse) that reduce environmental harm and align AI with climate and equity goals.
visual_elements: Lifecycle flow diagram showing resource and emissions hotspots: manufacture → training → deployment → end‑of‑life
Planetary‑boundary style gauge with an 'AI ecological budget' overlay to show safe vs. overshoot scenarios
Design trade‑off matrix (accuracy/utility vs. ecological cost) to guide model choices
Policy roadmap icon set showing levers: standards, procurement, reporting, caps/quotas
paper_title: A strong sustainability approach to AI development
